speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head J of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a small country, security is always a challenge.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If it comes to a war, it is generally assumed that a big, well-resourced country will prevail over a small one.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Unlike our neighbours who had larger populations, larger land mass and natural resources, when Singapore gained Independence, we were poor, had many pressing needs and competing challenges.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But the Government of the day knew that from the day we started, we needed a strong defence force and that there would be no economic future, no security without one.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thus, they invested in defence even though it was difficult.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This has been built on later with further important defence and training arrangements, including with other regional countries and big powers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These alliances have been built in the mutual best interest of all involved and Singapore needs to be a strong and valued partner in order for other countries to want to form alliances with us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Although our defence force remains strong and credible and our defence alliances strong, the security environment remains fraught with risks and uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As we had discussed in the earlier debate on foreign affairs, these threats are wide ranging and serious.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The threat of terrorism continues to spread with growing incidents of radicalised individuals and fighters returning from the Middle East to the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Attacks have taken place in major European cities but, closer to home, in Indonesia as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Korean Peninsula saw aggressive nuclear testing by North Korea barely a few months ago, and while ties remain warmer now, the nuclear risk remains.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Matters in the South China Sea have also calmed down a little, but there is no clear resolution in sight for the differences here, though, hopefully, parties can agree upon a code of conduct.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And today, security threats are increasingly taking on new forms, including self-radicalised terrorism and cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are complex and unpredictable, and take place below the threshold of war, and we may have to invest adequately to deal with such emergent threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While these threats linger, they take place against a backdrop of a risk that the US may reduce its role in the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, it is clear that we must continue to invest in defence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our Pioneer Generation had the foresight to invest in defence, and the "peace dividend" we have enjoyed over the last 50 years is the backdrop which has allowed Singapore to grow and thrive.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Today, we are one of the wealthiest countries in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Given our small size and the existential need for defence, defence spending has been a significant part of our Budget.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Defence expenditure has also been rising in the region in the face of growing security concerns, meaning all our regional neighbours are also building up their armed forces.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As forecasted in the Budget Debate earlier, we will be moving into a period when our population will be ageing and our needs for social spending will be rising at the same time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some have suggested, happily, not inside this House, cutting the defence Budget, a move that I would find worrying, given that security and defence are existential for us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What are Singapore's security plans in the face of the threats we face, and is our defence spending going to be adequate and sustainable in the face of these threats?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will SAF continue to support such global security and international peacekeeping efforts?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, terrorism has continued to pose a major threat to the peace and stability of our region.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: The scale of terror threats in our region has grown.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: It took a concerted effort between the Philippine Armed Forces and the Philippine National Police to recapture Marawi following five months of fierce fighting involving airstrikes and artillery fire.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Terror groups today have also operated with increasing coordination and sophistication, with operational linkages spanning across national borders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: The Maute group militants behind the Marawi siege had links with pro-ISIS cells and individuals in the region, and leveraged existing smuggling routes to move funds, people and arms through ungoverned spaces in the region.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: The Marawi siege in the Philippines showed us how militants can effectively organise themselves and pose a credible threat to homeland security forces.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: This underscores the importance of improving synergies across the whole-of-Government to ensure that there is a coordinated response to terrorist threats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: As such, how is the SAF coordinating with other Government agencies to prevent and respond to the threat of regional terrorism today?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There will also be other initiatives to help Singapore negotiate the current climate that we live in, which includes the Special Ops taskforce; the Army Deployment Force and, of course, the setup of the Island Defence Training Institute.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They are, indeed, major changes and they come with strategic investments and commitment as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What kind of scale of hardware and technological acquisition are we looking at?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How are our plans able to cover our land and sea borders as well as our air space in terms of attacks and threats?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We need to be ever ready to handle these extremely volatile situations, and how do we ensure that our men are all psychologically ready, knowing that they can be called upon anytime to protect Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: MINDEF also has broad goals for the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) chairmanship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister also share with us some of these, which include collaboration with ASEAN counterparts, including SAF and other Armed Forces that have got experience in dealing with a siege like the one in Marawi?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Imagine all our traffic light controls go haywire, with multiple accidents on the roads, our roads will become a logjam.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Airplanes above our heads can become weapons of mass destruction, like the 9-11 scenario.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our stock market and financial systems can be brought to a complete halt and all electronic financial transactions going astray.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our communication devices could be hacked and paralysing the entire country, making any rescue and recovery services impossible.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is a doomsday scenario that we frequently see in a Hollywood movie.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We read about many incidents of cyberattacks and breaches of security and cyber espionage around the world.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How prevalent are such attacks against Singapore, and how vulnerable are we?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What are we doing to protect Singapore from cyberattacks?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In recent years, cyberattacks have grown to be a major security concern.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In 2015, it was reported that the hackers had successfully compromised the information system of energy companies, leading to the temporary crippling of Ukraine's power grid.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Ukraine was again targeted in June 2017 with ransomware disrupting Ukraine's financial, energy and government sectors.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: At home, our Government education institutions are known to be hit by cyberattacks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Last year, our businesses, including several shopping malls, were affected by the "WannaCry" worm.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Fortunately, Singapore was less affected by the "WannaCry" worm, compared to some other countries.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: From these examples, it is clear that cyber-related threats can severely affect and disrupt Singaporeans' way of life.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: My question to the Minister is how prevalent are such attacks, how vulnerable are we and what is MINDEF doing to protect Singapore from cyberattacks?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, the growing availability of sophisticated tools on the Dark Web, designed to thwart secure systems, has greatly heightened the impetus to test and strengthen the security of our existing digital systems.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the same time, in our current fiscal climate of prudence, there is also a strong motivation to exercise good fiscal judgement.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This, I agree, is a sensible move to test its systems as it will be far cheaper than hiring a dedicated commercial cybersecurity vulnerability assessment team and potentially reveal weaknesses that may not be surfaced, given the very individual nature of white-hat hacking.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is the Bug Bounty Programme a one-off exercise or an ongoing engagement?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How does MINDEF's efforts fit into our national cybersecurity ecosystem?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: This highlights the current fiscal climate prudence as we face the "new normal" of slower growth rates.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: At the same time, we have witnessed an increase in the variety and danger of non-conventional threats to Singapore's security, in particular, in the cyber domain and by terrorists.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: MINDEF and SAF have invested resources to build our capabilities in these fields in the last few years.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Given the increasingly tight fiscal climate and the widening spectrum of threats that MINDEF and SAF now has to defend against, some worry that we may spread our defence dollars too thin.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: To fund the development of capabilities in emerging fields, MINDEF would likely have to exercise more prudence and possibly undertake some cost-cutting measures.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Could MINDEF elaborate on the specific prudence and cost-cutting measures that it is undertaking?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Today, Singapore faces new threats, such as terrorism and cyberattacks, in addition to the conventional threats.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Therefore, it is crucial that we transform and build new capabilities in our defence force to deter any potential aggressors and overcome any aggressors with a swift and potent defence force.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are good initiatives but do we have the manpower to do so in the future, especially when we are faced with a low birth rate?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will significantly grey the profile of our defence force.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many of these older ORNS may not be so tech savvy and will face difficulty in catching up with new technologies adopted by SAF.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thus, upgrading of these older ORNS to integrate into the defence force will be challenging.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this regard, I wish to seek clarifications from the Minister on the following: first, how SAF has leveraged technology to better equip our defence force; and second, update on the operational readiness of SAF for future threats.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, with Singapore's geographic location and size, we face several undisputable strategic realities, including our lack of strategic depth and weight, lack of natural resources and small population.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are critically dependent on the free flow of external trade, even as the open nature of our economy leaves us vulnerable to shifts and turbulence in the external environment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Given our vulnerabilities, we need to rely on both a strong SAF, as well as astute diplomacy, to protect our interests.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In particular, our involvement in regional security architecture is critical to fostering trust and cooperation and is essential to shaping a benign security environment within the region where Singapore can continue to grow and prosper.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Amidst the growing threats from extremists and the volatile geopolitical environment in the region, Singapore, as Chair of ADMM this year, is well-placed to advance the security interests of the region and Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In this regard, what are some of the initiatives that MINDEF is undertaking as ADMM Chair to achieve this?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, good progress is being made through the ADMM and ADMM-Plus frameworks to increase confidence among member countries and which lower but not eliminate the possibility and prospect of outright hostilities in the region, particularly over flashpoints, such as the South China Sea.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The upcoming ASEAN-China maritime exercise is a good example of the work that goes on to build confidence amongst each of the partner nations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In particular, the adoption of the Code for Unplanned Encounters at Sea (CUES) has raised hopes of its implementation even if an agreement amongst all the ADMM-Plus partners may prove to be harder to secure than the agreement of the ASEAN nations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is there any realistic prospect for a CUES framework for unplanned encounters in the air, as intimated by the Defence Minister last month, in view of fatal incidents in the past?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As ADMM Chair, it was reported that Singapore plans to strengthen cooperation and build resilience among the ASEAN member states and eight ADMM-Plus countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These include plans to increase counterterrorism collaboration and raising capabilities to combat chemical, biological and radiological threats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What has been the reception to this proposal by the ADMM and ADMM-Plus partners?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is, therefore, strategic for Singapore to minimise the tensions and prevent incidents and accidents from escalating into a serious event in the South China Sea.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We have a timely opportunity here to establish the framework to minimise the tensions.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is timely because Singapore is a non-claimant stakeholder in the settlement of the South China Sea disputes and has strong bilateral ties with many of the other stakeholders, including ASEAN countries, China and the US.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is also timely because the South China Sea disputes seem to be entering into a more rational phase of negotiation and balance of power, after the initial emotive phase occasioned by the jostling for territory.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In 2013, China and the US took part in a joint training exercise off Hawaii.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In 2014, both countries, along with other South China Sea stakeholders, signed the agreement on CUES.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: CUES is an excellent platform to work with to avoid the escalation of any incident and to maintain peace and stability in the South China Sea.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: One area is to affirm the importance of CUES on the sea and in the air.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is a worthy goal but, unfortunately, the press release was short on details about this area.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is excellent, as the US-China maritime exercise in 2013 fostered trust that led to the CUES agreement in 2014.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I am asking the latter question because 2018 is the beginning of the third ADMM-Plus three-year cycle and there were already four live exercises held in the last cycle which were useful for deepening regional security cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Chairman, let me thank the Members for their continued support to build up a strong defence for Singapore by voting for the financial policy of the Government yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This debate and the next on the Presidential Address after Parliament reopens are crucial.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For this debate, as expected, any proposed tax increase will attract attention.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If it did not, we would be in a different world, a surreal one.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But astute Members of Parliament (MPs) have pointed out that the financial Budget is but a means to an end.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As we deliberate on these key issues, we have to decide what we must never let go, lest we weaken the foundations of our growth, and what we must change to keep relevant with the times.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Those decisions from these two debates will affect every Singaporean, young or old, right or wrong.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Every Ministry, therefore, including and, especially defence, which takes up a large share of Government spending, must deal with these core issues.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Should we continue to put defence spending as a priority?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because, after all, we have had peace for 50 years and more now.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our relations with our neighbours are good on all sides.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have formed strong partnerships, as Members have pointed out, with major powers.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: How much should we invest in building a strong SAF and how much can we afford?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Past generations did so even when there were many competing needs.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We talked about our rising needs but, past generations, as a Third-World country, in Singapore, our needs then were dire and everywhere – houses, schools, hospitals, roads, public facilities, jobs – all in short supply.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because our military capabilities at Independence were next to nothing, the Government of the day had to make hard decisions – every dollar spent on building up the military was a dollar taken from other needs.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And yet, they paid the price to build up a strong SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew and the Pioneer Generation, who lived through Singapore as a British colony, under Japanese occupation and as part of Malaysia, held a deep conviction on self-determination through a strong defence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: At the National Day Parade (NDP) which Members here attend, we replay a particular clip of Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is a very stern admonition and, in this coming NDP, I invite you to listen to it again.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It was uttered in 1967 when NS was introduced, "If you, who are growing up, do not understand that you have got to defend this, then I say, in the end, we will lose.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Other people will come, smack you down, take it over." I cannot say it as harshly as Mr Lee because that generation lived through difficult times.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is just unnatural for us, but when he says it, and when the Pioneer Generation says it, it is so authentic.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Harsh words for harsh times, but ever so necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Not only for that generation, but I think for every generation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, listen to that clip again this year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: With that deep conviction and sacrificial commitment, we, today, have a modern and professional SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: From two infantry battalions – which, if you read Mr Lee's memoirs, were still under Malaysian command even after we separated – we now have an Army, combined arms divisions, fully manned and able to move at short notice.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Many Members here are NSmen and had gone through MOBEX.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As they went to the counters, these were automated counters, where a camera takes a picture of you, recognises you, issues you a slip to say which company and platoon you go to, and what your role is, and what weapons you need to draw.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But you actually do not have to draw the weapons because, at the same time, when it is activated, we did not cheat, we activated both sides, from our ammunition storage facilities, they are activated.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And they pushed weapons, platforms, to meet up with the men.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: That should give a lot of confidence to Members in this House and Singaporeans outside.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Republic of Singapore (RSAF) commemorates its Golden Jubilee this year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But when it started, we had two Cessnas.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We leased them from the Singapore Flying Club.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And when I say that, it means that we have pilots on standby.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because after 9-11, we took that threat seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If there are planes that come to us unplanned, our fighter planes are mobilised.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It takes a while to get mobilised, so our chaps are there.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: From time to time, we gently guide errant, sometimes, lost pilots, down to the field.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But you never know when there might be a real attack, just like 9-11.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our Navy started with two wooden hull boats, probably sinkable if attacked.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We now have a modern Navy of Littoral Mission Vessels (LMVs), frigates and submarines that protect our waters and maritime hub.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The commitment of previous generations to build up a strong SAF was not merely through words or aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It required substantial financial resources from the Government and the people.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But that was not the only and, in fact, not the most precious resource they had to give.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They gave of themselves, as every Singaporean male, as every male MP in this House who has done NS, has done so, through NS, with the full support from family and employers.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The results of that unequivocal commitment are plain for everyone to see – to Singaporeans, to our neighbours and, indeed, globally – an SAF today that is able to defend Singapore, but beyond that, an SAF that has contributed to global security.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As Mr Vikram Nair said, how do we show that we are a valued partner?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It went beyond our wildest imagination that SAF troops and assets, as Mr Teo Ser Luck pointed out, were helping in Hurricane Harvey in Texas and, before that, Hurricane Katrina; or could be deployed as peacekeepers in Timor-Leste or against terrorism in Afghanistan and Iraq; against pirates in the Gulf of Aden; and in humanitarian efforts in Aceh and Nepal.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Who would have thought of it when SAF was started more than 50 years ago?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Yes, we will continue to do this because the partnerships forged from playing our role internationally are important in dealing with transnational threats that affect our own security.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We are not playing "good guy", to be honest.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It raises our stakes, our value to others who want then to help us as we deal with transnational security threats.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It has been the steady investments in defence spending that enabled these achievements by a strong SAF, both locally and internationally.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This is a Committee of Supply (COS) debate.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, I think some details of actual financing are appropriate.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have handed out, with your permission, Mr Chairman, charts and these are also shown on the screens.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The first figure shows our defence spending for the last 30 years.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: First off, in blue, is the percentage of Government expenditure – how much MINDEF spends as a part of Government expenditure.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So much for Singapore's spending, but defence must always be seen in perspective.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: What you spend is never as important as what everyone else spends.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, let us see the next slide – what is the defence spending by countries around us?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I have chosen just to focus on ASEAN but I think probably the same can be said of Asia, ex ASEAN and Singapore, and even more.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In the last decade, our ASEAN neighbours have been spending more.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In the last decade, our ASEAN neighbours have been spending more to modernise their defence capabilities even as their economies grew.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And even for the next decade, MINDEF does not foresee any spike in defence spending.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Obviously, this will not apply if there are exigencies or unexpected scenarios.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For instance, if there is a terrorist attack or if the security environment deteriorates, our agencies will have to spend more to protect Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And after the next decade, I think it would be prudent for the Government of that day and this House to reassess the security threats and the military spending, and the capabilities of other countries and plan ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, if Members can remember and are still in this House 10 years hence in 2028 and beyond, please remember this gentle admonition, sound out warnings if you think necessary, for those of you privileged to be in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Two crucial lessons learnt from our experiences as well as that from negative examples from other countries who went the other way, and they are: first, the best time to prepare for trouble is during peace; second, in the long run, steady investments into military capabilities maintain peace through deterrence and result in more effective outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is actually the most efficient yield for defence investments.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In other words, even if you spent the same dollar amount over a defined period and one was gentle and smooth, and the other went up and down, the most effective yield is continuous steady investments, and I will tell Members why, by examples, which many European countries have learnt in bitter ways.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I recently spoke of how Lithuania did away with NS after the Cold War, but has now to reintroduce it following the annexation of Crimea.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Just think – one Defence Minister decides, "alright, National Service is no longer necessary".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The same one, or a few years later, another one decides, "let us reintroduce it".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Certainly not in time to deal with an imminent crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: People are asking France and Germany, who are the two largest powers, to do more.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: President Macron, to his credit, believes it should be done, but they have to up their defence spending by 40%.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I have not calculated how much it affects their defence spending.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It would have to go up to €50 billion, an increase of €16 billion in seven years.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Not only a 2% increase in GST would help; probably a 3%, 4% or 5% hike in GST just to pay for the increase in defence spending.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Germany, even with its troubled past, is now asked by the European Union (EU) states to do more militarily.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I have attended the Munich Security Dialogue, as Defence Ministers in Singapore have, for the past decade or more.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And, at that time, there was almost a schizophrenia. "We think we want Germany to do more but with your troubled past, maybe you should not do more." That debate is done.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But after 25 years of cuts to the German defence budget, the German military – the Bundeswehr – is underfunded, with entire weapons systems unusable, because they either lack spare parts or have been poorly maintained.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The platforms are there but only half can be activated.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When the Aceh tsunami occurred, we activated three of our four Landing Ship Tanks (LSTs).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It happened on Boxing Day – no way you could have had prior warning.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: On activation, all moved – 75% of the assets of that particular platform.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The fourth was in the Gulf, as Deputy Prime Minister Teo has reminded me.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If we had to send another one, we would have to borrow it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Bundeswehr will need many years to modernise its platforms and make up for lost time.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When I share these lessons, I say these are salutary lessons that we must voraciously imbibe, because someone else has paid to learn them.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But we have to prioritise and focus and optimise our resources.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some Members have asked about counterterrorism – Assoc Prof Dr Muhd Faishal, Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF takes terrorism very seriously, so much so that we have to reorganise, train and equip differently.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members have pointed out, including Dr Teo Ho Pin, how we now train.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have the capacity to train 18,000 SAF NSmen for homeland security.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We learned very valuable lessons from Marawi, another painful lesson that someone else learnt.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I made a trip, Deputy Prime Minister Teo made a trip recently, where they found out and they admitted that they underestimated the problem, both the number of fighters and how well they were equipped.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Snipers had good weapons, heavy machine guns, and they even had anti-tank weapons.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The terrorists conducted urban warfare against soldiers and policemen of the Philippine authorities who were not trained for that kind of fight.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: That is why it took five months for the Philippine armed forces and homeland security to dislodge the militants from that city.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And this, after many lives lost and the city devastated.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I think the bill they have recently estimated will cost about US$2 billion.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The experiences there confirm that SAF is on the right track in building up our counterterrorism capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I have talked about Singapore Armed Forces Training Institute (SAFTI) City last year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When completed, it will allow our soldiers to train more realistically for homeland security and counterterrorism because it will be a different Pasir Laba that you and I were used to.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Buildings, I do not know how high you can build it, but at least higher than what we have now, and to teach them how to fight in that kind of scenario.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members rightly pointed out that we have to do more with other Government agencies to respond to these terror threats.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We are working together with the Police's Frontline Policing Training Centre.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We will conduct joint training and equip NSmen with the skills to perform these homeland security operations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: At sea, various agencies are coordinated, whether it is the Navy, Police Coast Guard, Maritime and Port Authority (MPA) or Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA), so that we keep our waters safe.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But as much as we prepare at home, Singapore needs to be part of the international effort to deal with terrorism at its source.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: That is a sound strategy because, if you do not do that, you are just dealing with the problem too late and you allow the problem to mushroom.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We did that against Al-Qaeda, from 2007, in Afghanistan, after which the threat has dissipated for now.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our SAF troops have been deployed in Iraq since 2014 against ISIS and with considerable progress.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The coalition effort, led by the US, has taken Iraq back from ISIS control.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: US Secretary of Defense James Mattis wrote to me recently to ask Singapore to commit more resources for the next phase of consolidation after our hard-won victories.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef suggested, we need to work with ASEAN on counterterrorism, and some others have pointed that out too, including Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Low Thia Khiang, especially because the risk of foreign fighters leaving Iraq and Syria has gone up.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, paradoxically, as the problem there diminishes, they run away; and they come back, whether it is Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines or even Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Philippine Special Operations Command came to Singapore last December for a two-week professional exchange and our offer to the Philippines Armed Force to use our unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for surveillance remains open.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo, when he visited Philippine leaders, reiterated that offer, too, recently.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF stands ready to join the Sulu Seas patrol when invited.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As ADMM Chair, we recently proposed a counterterrorism framework – there were many programmes but we felt we needed a comprehensive framework and we devised the 3Rs – the equivalent to reading, writing, arithmetic.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Rather, it is "Resilience, Response, Recovery", to coordinate our responses to prevent, deal with and recover from attacks.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked about the growing cyber threat, indeed, a transnational threat with effects that could be devastating as physical attacks, whether it is power grids, whether it is financial grids, whether it is hospitals, and so on and so forth.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: At the whole-of-Government level, Deputy Prime Minister Teo chairs our Coordinating Inter-Ministerial Committee, the Security Policy Committee.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But at the Ministry level, we are responsible for our own Ministries as well as the ecosystem in which that Ministry is in charge of.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members have asked who the attacks come from, how often and whom they are targeted at.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I think Members can guess at the answer.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The attacks are conducted by freelancers, as well as organised state and non-state actors.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Senior MINDEF and SAF leaders, as well as departments handling sensitive information have been deliberately targeted, for example, by "spear-phishing".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Those of you in information technology (IT) will know what this is.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In other words, you get innocent-looking emails addressed to you, but it contains malicious software.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If you click on the attachment, or sometimes even when you click on the email – I do not think they have reached a stage where you look at it and the malicious software might come.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They have not succeeded, but they will keep trying.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As we do in the physical arena, MINDEF adopts a multi-layered approach to cyber defence, including the ultimate step of physically separating sensitive systems from the Internet.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Internally, there is a system – we do not want to talk to you, please do not come in.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have "red teams” which are testing for vulnerabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari asked about our Bug Bounty programme.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It attracted 260 white-hat hackers, all bona fide, and improved our systems at relatively low cost.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have shared lessons with other agencies, like the Government Technology Agency (GovTech) and the Cyber Security Agency (CSA), and the results are encouraging.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I do not think it is a one-off.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It may not be an exact mould, but we will think of these ways to crowdsource.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For the Internet, we can do it; we can crowdsource and actually leverage off that connectivity.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As Members have pointed out, we will build up a cyber force with more SAF regulars and full-time staff.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This year, we will take in the pilot batch of full-time National Servicemen (NSFs) under the Cyber NSF Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For those of you who have friends, children or children of friends who are interested and suitable, tell them about this.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For those interested and suitable, we will offer them regular contracts of varying durations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If they accept, we will also invest more on training them.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We will also set up a cyber defence training and exercise infrastructure to train them.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, this is long term, needs a long-term plan, and we have begun.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Teo Ser Luck asked how we can be prudent in spending, and he is spot on.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have to be prudent, but we will not compromise.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF will not compromise our defence capabilities but we have found ways to optimise resources.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We want to stretch every dollar, where we can.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have used innovation and better work processes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For instance, our new LMVs will cost around $65 million less for the whole fleet to maintain across their lifetime.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: LMVs are much more capable than the Petrol Vessels but will cost less.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because they have less crew, they are more efficient to maintain.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The RSAF’s aerostat, our big balloon – yesterday, there were some discussions about floating balloons – let me just say that when SAF floats balloons, it is there to stay, and it is meant to be up.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF upgrades existing equipment, where possible, to avoid buying new platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our first instinct is not to buy, but to upgrade.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And that is what we did for our whole fleet of Leopard Tanks and Chinooks.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We must harness new technologies, as Dr Teo Ho Pin pointed out.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because even if you chose to give us more money in exchange for manpower, we cannot do it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We recognise that as an inherent constraint, and we started to deal with it, I think, probably one or even two decades ago, in terms of redesigning our systems, in terms of maintaining our systems.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin mentioned that the older ORNS, those in their 60s, would not be so adept.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We are not planning to induct them into our Armed Forces, because their liability ends at 40 to 50.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Of those who are in our Order of Battle (ORBAT), there are some examples.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For example, it will use drones to perform runway damage assessment.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members will notice, for instance, at the recent Air Show, it is beautiful to watch, and people clap in glee, but after the fighter planes take off or land, we have to do visual checks to make sure that the commercial planes can come in, too.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Same thing for each take-off; you have to do visual checks because even small debris make a difference.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We can use drones to perform runway damage assessment and respond to other intruding drones.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We want to make it more efficient by leveraging automation for aircraft maintenance and using sensors for pre- and post-flight aircraft checks.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I think it is achievable and we are doing trials to achieve that kind of Smart Airbase.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Navy is integrating data from all agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The maritime environment is a different environment from the air.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There are lots of moving parts and different agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We want to gather data from all sources, construct better algorithms to detect anomalies and then pre-empt, say, possible terrorist threats from the sea.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For surveillance, we want to use cameras with smart sensors with automated surveillance.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We do not need a man in the loop, or a man in every loop, to say, “this vessel is behaving in a different way from other vessels”.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, just alert you, so that when the man in the loop makes a decision, you respond.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We do not need manned vessels for some scenarios.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: All these give us hope that we are moving towards an SAF that is just as, or even more effective, but can use less manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We agree wholeheartedly with Members here who pointed out that we cannot do this alone.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have to join other partners or other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Jessica Tan, Mr Low Thia Khiang, Mr Pritam Singh, thank you for affirming that what we decided as ADMM Chair this year is important.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We said that there will be three areas: first, counterterrorism; second, confidence-building measures and code for unplanned encounters at sea and in the air; and third, chemical, biological and radiological threats.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: That was really precipitated because of the Korean Peninsula instability, and most countries are not prepared for those kinds of threats.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As Members pointed out rightly, CUES has been accepted.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: What is the possibility of a CUES for air being accepted, is a tough one, I agree.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But if we can do it across 18 nations, I think that will send a very strong signal.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We will at least start the ball rolling and see whether we can get consensus from the 10 ASEAN countries and the Plus-eight.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I think among some of them, they will be more willing.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And if we can talk to them and say, "This works for you", I think we would have done a significant contribution.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some asked about the exercise, Mr Low and Mr Pritam Singh as well, whether we are practising CUES.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And in 2018, I suspect, this year, with China, it may be in undisputed waters, so there would not be a chance to practise it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Member asked whether the meetings of the ADMM-Plus will be yearly.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They have agreed and Singapore will be the first to host these annual meetings.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: With the US, we have achieved new milestones.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Both the Republic of Singapore Navy (RSN) and RSAF conducted bilateral exercises in Guam for the first time last year, flying with US Pacific Air Forces (PACAF) and exercising across the full spectrum of anti-submarine, anti-surface and anti-air warfare with the US Navy.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: With China, we will build on the positive momentum from the visit of Chinese Defence Minister Chang Wanquan early this year and we have deepened ties with the People's Liberation Army (PLA).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: With India, we concluded a Navy Bilateral Agreement and we will increase maritime security cooperation between our countries, especially around the Andaman Seas.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We will build strong partnerships, but all of us here know that, ultimately, we, Singaporeans, must be accountable for our own defence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When we are dependent on others, we have failed.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our NSmen will be better trained through new facilities in the SAFTI City and in Australia.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: With continued investments steady, year after year, which Members of this House approve, SAF will continue its transformation onwards.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our territorial waters and sea lines of communications will be better secured with manned and unmanned vessels alike.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In doing so, we have kept faith with what we were entrusted with by previous generations – a strong SAF able to ensure our independence and protect Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But that a strong SAF was not built or maintained by happenstance or even good intentions.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For each generation, it will require a conscious, deliberate decision.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It will require sacrifices to commit resources and of themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As Mr Lee Kuan Yew said to SAF officers at a Temasek Society dinner in 2012, “From the day we started, I knew that we needed a strong SAF and I believe that still remains today.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If each generation reaffirms and renews its commitment, then a strong SAF will continue to keep Singapore safe and sovereign with a secure future for another generation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Potential adversaries know that when they want to attack Singapore, it is a fight against all of us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The political atmospherics in the region have waxed and waned over the years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As we now enjoy warm and friendly relations with all our ASEAN partners, some segments of our society have questioned if NS remains relevant in this context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: After all, the probability of conventional conflict is perceived to be remote.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Recognising that NS is premised on the need for national defence, can MINDEF elaborate on the role that NS plays in Singapore today and its importance, given prevailing geopolitical conditions?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: However, several trends in recent years have threatened the size of the SAF's enlistment pool, chief among them, the trend of our falling birth rate and the ageing population.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: In view of these impending manpower constraints, what are the manpower challenges faced by SAF?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: What measures are being taken to ensure that these manpower challenges will not compromise our overall military capability?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Like many of my male colleagues in this House, we have fond memories of NS, and NS is the rite of passage for all Singaporean males, regardless of background, and only in NS we get to mix around with peers of different backgrounds, different status and come together and work together.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So, besides preparing our young people, our young men, for operations, it also has an important role in enhancing social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: NS, in that sense, is an integral part of our society.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And what is SAF doing to build more common experiences and improve cohesion between NSFs from different walks of life during their service?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, despite our best efforts, our attempts to increase the birth rate have a limited impact so far.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This has serious implications for our economy and also our security.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we look to the future, manpower challenges will mean that each individual that serves NS becomes increasingly precious, both during service and after.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During service, each individual will now have a bigger role to play as the total number of servicemen and women decline due to smaller cohorts.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: After service, we need to ensure that all Singaporeans are equipped to thrive in the new world of work.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We will struggle as a nation if all our males are two years behind their counterparts in the acquisition of skills they need in order to survive in the workplace of the future.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This aims to offer a more positive, fulfilling and meaningful NS experience for our servicemen.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: At the same time, it encourages our NSmen to take greater ownership of their roles, responsibilities and contributions in ensuring Singapore's safety and security.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I checked out the Central Manpower Base (CMPB) website and found that the videos and handbook on the 33 NS vocations in SAF, the Singapore Police Force (SPF) and the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) very useful.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This will provide greater insights for our young pre-enlistees to make more informed choices.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I note that the final posting results will look at factors, such as physical fitness, suitability to perform tasks and operational requirements, besides the interests of the new enlistees.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: How have the interests been matched, and the response of the enlistees?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Investigations revealed that some attackers employed sophisticated anti-detection and infection techniques to access information through cyber backdoors.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have all heard from Defence Minister Ng Eng Hen just earlier.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He spoke about the threats that are posed by malware emails.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, these developments demonstrate that cyber threats to Singapore are becoming more sophisticated, making detection and forensic investigation more difficult.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Not surprisingly, MINDEF was targeted by deliberate hacking attempts on its Internet-facing system early last year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given our small population and geographical size, SAF relies heavily on digitisation and networking in our capabilities to achieve a military edge against our potential adversaries.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, these military networks and systems and the sensitive information they contain make them an attractive target of cyberattacks.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How sustainable will the scheme be, given the much talked about reduction in the population size, thus a smaller number of NSFs available?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Mr Chairman, technology is evolving at an accelerating pace and has the potential to make our lives better in ways that would have been unimaginable just a few years ago.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: We can now effortlessly try how much physical activities we do, where we go and whom we interact with.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: The data that we capture can be mined to provide insights into almost every aspect of human life.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: This technology can be used to improve the effectiveness and safety of NS training or, at the same time, helping individual serviceman to develop useful skills.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: For example, advances in virtual reality and related fields enable us to create new types of training.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Individual troops can practise critical skills in a safe environment and commanders can try out different strategies to see which one will work best.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: The potential to apply technology to NS is limited only by our imagination and our willingness to take the lead.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: We can improve training outcomes whilst reducing risks to our servicemen.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, since its introduction in 1967, NS has remained the cornerstone of Singapore's defence, providing the security and stability which underpin our shared prosperity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To date, more than a million have served NS and NS has become deeply entrenched as a national institution.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Going forward, it is important that this institution continues to enjoy the strong support of every Singaporean in every household and in every community.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over the past four years, the family and community council within the Advisory Council on Community Relations in Defence (ACCORD) had developed initiatives to strengthen community support for total defence and NS.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of these initiatives include (a) the engagement of new citizens and Permanent Residents (PRs) to understand the need for defence and support the NS institution; and (b) the partnership with the Singapore Armed Forces Reservists Association (SAFRA) and the People's Association (PA) to encourage retailers to offer discounts to NSmen in recognition of their service to the nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Military service is tough and the sacrifices are real for our NSmen who spent time away from their careers and loved ones in defence of our nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What else can MINDEF and ACCORD do to educate the public on the sacrifices of our NSmen and galvanise community support for these men serving our country?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Mr Chairman, my cut is on MINDEF’s efforts to recognise the contributions of our NSmen and the initiatives undertaken by ACCORD to increase the public’s awareness of NS.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: SAF underwrites Singapore’s sovereignty upon which all Singaporeans can live in peace, and secure in the knowledge that Singapore is well-protected.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: NS is a duty for all male Singaporeans and second-generation PRs.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: It is the cornerstone of Singapore’s defence and security.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: For many Singaporean males, NS is a rite of passage at about 18 years of age, where he leaves the comforts of home and takes on the commitment of defending his country, his family and friends.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: After the initial two years of full-time commitment in NS, the NSF transitions to ORNS duties as NSmen, and this is about 10 years in length.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: During this time, our NSmen will have to juggle career and family commitments as well as their national defence duties.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Therefore, it would be right and necessary for us to recognise the contributions of our NSmen.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Just last year, we celebrated NS50, where the whole nation came together to thank successive generations of NSmen for their contributions to our nation’s defence over the years.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Singaporeans from all walks of life took the opportunity to recommit themselves to play their part to protect our Independence, values and way of life.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I am sure that many of our NSmen, past and present, benefited from the various NS50 promotions and offers, generously supported by the private sector as well, who understood the importance of national defence.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Yet, this widespread show of support across the public and private spheres should not be a one-off or should not be limited to milestone years alone.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Our NSmen must continue to know that their sacrifices to serve NS are appreciated and not taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Hence, I would like to ask the Minister how has MINDEF continued in its efforts to recognise the contributions of our NSmen.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Many of these knowledge and skills, such as leadership, planning, command and control or safety measures, are applicable when the NSmen join the workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Defence spending must keep up with Singapore's partnerships and match the growing sophisticated needs of our advanced economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Like all areas of Government, defence spending will be put under pressure in years to come.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In anticipation of this, defence spending must keep up with the state of the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This includes the area of manpower use and productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Strength and resilience of an economy are based on, among other things, a workforce which embraces productive and efficient work practices and habits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Full-time NS is a major milestone in our young people's lives, often the most significant initial encounter with a regulated work environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Even for those who deferred entry into the labour force after NS because of studies or other pursuits, the concentrated immersion in full-time NS work cultures so early in their adulthood exerts a major influence over the attitudes of young people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It will help to ensure the sacrifice of time and effort made by young people in full-time NS have a continuing relevance to their working lives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I have three questions for the Minister: what is the role of full-time NS in shaping the work ethic of young Singaporeans?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What does NS contribute to promoting an awareness of the importance of productivity performance and efficiency at both the individual and organisational levels?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And, finally, what are the possibilities for coordinating regimentation in the Armed Forces with productivity and efficiency?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Singaporeans are familiar with the five pillars as we commemorate Total Defence Day on 15 February every year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: These are aimed at breaking societies from within by exploiting our social fault lines to weaken national unity, erode trust in Government and diminish confidence in the nation's future.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: At the same time, Singapore society is also evolving.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This growing diversity may give rise to new potential fault lines and make it more difficult for us to maintain social harmony.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Against this backdrop, Singapore's approach of Total Defence has proven to be a remarkable presence and also provided a bulwark against such insidious threats.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Can MINDEF provide an update on its 2018 Total Defence campaign and how we intend to address these threats, going forward?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Chairman, on most objective measures, we are living in the best of times in history.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: With declining poverty and hunger and falling rates of death due to disease and war, yet countries are also faced with growing threats to their economies and their ways of life.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: The most obvious and high profile are, of course, terrorist attacks, such as 9-11 or the London bombings.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: But just as dangerous to the long-term health of the nation are most subtle forms of threats, such as the ramping up of social and societal tensions through propaganda and fake news.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: We have seen that even mature western democracies are not immune to this form of cyber-psycho terrorism with foreign activists leveraging social media to provoke both sides on issues that divide society, such as racism, inequality or gun rights.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: These threats are not easy to define or detect and even more difficult to fight.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: We are proud of our multiracial, multi-religious global society here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: We may worship different gods and practise different cultures and traditions, but we live in peace and harmony in this compact Little Red Dot.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Our status as a global hub has helped grow our economy and added to the vibrancy of our nation.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: However, we are also aware that we cannot take all these for granted.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: If we look overseas, we can see how race, religion and immigration issues can affect not only society and politics but also result in terrorism and violence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: These terrorists will use race and religion as a “socio-weapon” to tear people apart.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore, we are not immune to the threat of terrorism, and we know that there are people in recent years that have been self-radicalised.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: In Europe and the US, we have witnessed the manifestations of globalisation backlash in US politics, Brexit and the rise of anti-immigration parties in Europe.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: As these threats exploit the fault lines in our increasingly diverse society to divide our people, what can we, as Singaporeans, do as part of Total Defence to strengthen social cohesiveness and affirm multiculturalism to fortify our defences against the scourge of terrorism and in the face of other external pressures?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This means that Singaporeans are also more easily exposed to false news and pressures found online, which could tear our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The threat of fake news is pervasive and insidious.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: On social media, articles and stories usually go viral and get circulated because they are sensational or they corroborate one's own beliefs and views.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: However, it is not always possible to verify the truth of stories being circulated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This makes it fertile grounds for the spreading of fake news.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: To make matters worse, fake news is also usually profitable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Revenues generated online are usually correlated to eyeballs and circulation, not the truth or quality of the stories involved.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: One just needs to share sensational stories without having to pay journalists to actually investigate and report the truth.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Thus, in an environment where purveyors can make profits by keeping costs low and getting wide circulation, traditional media companies that do real investigation and report real news, which is usually less sensational, are suffering, with readerships dropping for traditional news providers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This is a double whammy because it means that fake news ends up circulating, while real news requires paid subscriptions, is suffering and struggles to counteract the fake news.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Our Foreign Minister had very kindly confirmed that this was the case in Singapore as well, but he was probably too diplomatic to name the state actors involved.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The most shocking of the recent allegations, in fact, occurred in the greatest power, the US, where allegations are being made in some quarters in the US that there was Russian interference in their elections.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: It is already common ground that there was a great deal of fake news being circulated in the last US elections, with candidates on both sides being victims of fake news stories.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: If so, what steps does MINDEF intend to take to combat threats from fake news?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Its main mission is to serve in assigned roles alongside SAF NSFs, NSmen and regulars to enhance the security of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: SAFVC is also a great opportunity for citizens from diverse backgrounds to meet, train and bond together.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Mr Chairman, the world today is characterised by the rise of the Internet and globalisation.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Our youths will grow up and mature in an environment that will grant them access to an immense variety of views and experiences.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: While this opens up many opportunities for education and a deeper appreciation for diversity, it will also likely reshape their sense of identity in new ways.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: In particular, their understanding of what it means to be “Singaporean” will no longer be strongly defined only by an understanding of Singapore’s history, culture and our vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: However, Singaporeans’ commitment towards defending our country rests on whether we possess a good understanding of our vulnerabilities and an ingrained conviction of the importance of what we are defending.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: While it is important to instill this understanding in our youths from a young age, growing global interconnectivity and the ensuing potential dilution of the “Singapore Identity” will continue to pose a strong challenge to our efforts.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I note that MINDEF has used many innovative and interesting ways to engage the public of different age groups on Total Defence, for example, N.E.mation! video competition, "Guardians of the City" strategy card game, Total Defence (TD) Badge Programme, TD Puzzle, colouring activity and documentary-drama series "It Will Never Happen Here".

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: How has MINDEF’s experience been these years and how could MINDEF reach out better to youths today to deepen their understanding of Total Defence and encourage them to play their part?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: It has moved on from just being a defence imperative to being a cultural institution, which is a part of Singapore's national identity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Moving ahead, our falling birth rate will pose a significant challenge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: This may mark a timing for decision to utilise more technology, unmanned systems and so on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: The technological disruption will not spare the area of defence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Do we have personnel who are highly trained in these areas and can they train others?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: How are we preparing our young recruits for this?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Chairman, besides the community at large, families also play a very important role in supporting our NSmen.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: At the individual level, families are the primary source of moral, emotional and social support for our NSmen.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Strong families will be able to pick up signs of emotional or psychological stress in our NSmen and seek assistance before such pressure escalates.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: At the national level, families sustain NS as a national institution as they continue to encourage successive generations of Singaporean sons to undergo the rite of passage that is NS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I thank the members for all their questions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dr Maliki Osman and I will try to answer all of them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last year, we commemorated 50 years of NS in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Assoc Prof Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim asked about the continued importance of NS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It remains the bedrock of the strong and credible SAF that we have today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Their and their families’ sacrifices keep our country safe and secure and, as Singaporeans, we can decide our future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One of our greatest defence assets is that Singaporeans are strongly behind NS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Cedric Foo asked about this, and that this cannot be one-off, just a one-time good feeling during NS50, but sustained support for NS for the long term.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some countries, in fact, struggle to maintain public support for their conscription systems.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Minister Ng Eng Hen mentioned Lithuania; another example is Sweden, which got rid of NS a decade ago, only to have to reinstate it as they re-evaluate their security environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
