text: I think Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked about that, too.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think Mr Amrin Amin asked about this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the imperative is to do more with less, to work with fewer but more capable servicemen.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The future capability and effectiveness of SAF will not be based on the number and quantity of people we have.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, it will be based on their quality and ability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will achieve this by enhancing three things.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One, individual ability; two, strengthening system efficiency; and three, leveraging technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The foundation for operational readiness is, first and foremost, physical fitness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fitness is also very personal, unique to the individual, with its impact on the individual’s health extending well beyond their time with SAF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will leverage technology to deliver targeted and effective training for every serviceman.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The new CESP ‒ Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked about it ‒ is adopting a scientific, data-driven approach to optimise the performance of every soldier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is the key purpose of the Centre.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It uses wearables and data to better understand each individual soldier’s physiological condition, and then prescribe more effective and progressive training, while minimising the risk of acute injury.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The training can, in fact, be customised to what the soldier is supposed to do and what their vocation and task are.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, it is the granularity that we can now administer training to fit a soldier's physiological condition as well as his responsibility.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will also provide servicemen with better tools to keep fit and increase the choices and accessibility of fitness training.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are partnering SportSG and the Health Promotion Board (HPB) to introduce the Quick High Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) Programme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: NSmen will be able to attend the Quick HIIT programme at community spaces and sports facilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Starting this week, we are also piloting the use of wearable technology at SAF Fitness Conditioning Centres and SAFRA gyms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, rather than adhering strictly to the SAF-conducted Individual Physical Proficiency Test (IPPT) Preparatory Training (IPT) regime, NSmen will now be able to choose the type of exercise they prefer or need.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They can cycle, run, do weights or interval training and then clock in their fitness progress via wearable devices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And as long as they achieve the required calories and intensity ‒ we measure only the output but we do not measure the input ‒ we will consider it a valid IPT session.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a significant shift, giving NSmen choice, convenience and empowerment in improving their fitness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After all, fitness is an individual, not an SAF, responsibility.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Individuals can only be effective if units are cohesive and servicemen have a strong sense of camaraderie forged through common experiences, which Mr Teo Ser Luck asked about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: BMT is a large part of this shared NS experience.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Since the establishment of the Basic Military Training Centre (BMTC) in 1987, it has become ‒ as Mr Teo Ser Luck put it ‒ a rite of passage for many male Singaporeans to complete basic training "overseas" – on Pulau Tekong.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, many NSFs do not go through BMTC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are enlisted directly into combat units, in what is commonly known as mono-intake units.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These NSFs will benefit from BMTC’s dedicated training experience, infrastructure and use of technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Most importantly, they will share a common experience, within the unit, as well as within the larger SAF tribe.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A second major thrust is to strengthen system efficiency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This means improving the way the system deploys the right serviceman to the right job, to maximise his contribution and potential.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The most important initiative under this thrust is the review of vocation requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon asked about using technology to maximise the potential of servicemen.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Indeed, it is because of technology that we are now in a position to review vocation requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With technology, you can no longer draw a firm line between combat-fit and non-combat fit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Take, for example, the personnel operating autonomous systems in the control room.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are in combat, even though they are not physically exerting.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, many more servicemen can now perform what could have only been done by servicemen who used to have to meet the most stringent physical requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, physical requirements and demands for vocations, such as combat engineers and security troopers, are now much less as we leverage technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This has opened up opportunities for us to more meaningfully deploy NSmen according to their fitness and abilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng asked about the Vocation Interest initiative, where pre-enlistees will indicate their interest in 33 NS vocations across the SAF, SCDF and SPF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is no guarantee that servicemen will get the vocations they indicated interest in, because the primary consideration is still our defence operational requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we will take their interests into consideration during the deployment process and try our best to match them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng mentioned that one group has passed their BMT and asked for an update.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Next week, they will have their Passing Out Parade, out of BMT.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: More than 80% of those surveyed felt that the initiative encouraged them to take greater ownership of their NS roles and responsibilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many asked for tough vocations, like Infantry and Guards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will continue to refine and improve the system as we go along.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are also leveraging NSFs' talent in niche areas, such as cybersecurity, through the Cyber NSF Scheme, which Ms Low Yen Ling asked for an update.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There has been an overwhelmingly positive response since I announced the scheme, with numerous pre-enlistees writing in to express interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we will be putting the applicants through a rigorous selection test on their skills and aptitudes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will not look at their academic grades so much.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The scheme has been launched as a pilot trial for those enlisting in the latter half of this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In recent years, we have taken many leaps forward.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Minister Ng Eng Hen has given a few examples.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another example will be our Smart naval bases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon asked about leveraging technology to enhance the NS experience.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Indeed, besides enabling manpower savings, such technologies can also create wonders on the ground, make NS a better experience, and raise morale.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last year, we introduced an e-fitting system at CMPB.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Pre-enlistees no longer have to go through the tedious process of measuring all their body dimensions manually.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will now be done by infrared body and foot scanners to quickly and accurately fit pre-enlistees to their uniforms and sports shoes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are embarking on a trial to further enhance the experience at CMPB during pre-enlistment screening.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By using facial recognition and real-time queue management technology, we will optimise visitor flow and shorten waiting times.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another innovation, which is quite cute, is an AI-enabled chatbot called "NS Buddy".

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I never had this when I was an NSman.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At any time of the day, the serviceman could pose a question to the NS Buddy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, he can ask "What is BTP?" The Buddy will then explain that it stands for Basic Train-fire Package.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then it will present the facts, and then also give advice to say “aim properly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Safety First!” We will be enhancing the NS Buddy in the next phase of the trial, expanding its content base, and adding more SAF lexicons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, for NS to continue to be the cornerstone of Singapore's defence, we need Singaporeans' support.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Cedric Foo asked about the community's support for NS and recognition for NSmen.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many of us must be heartened to witness the high level of public participation in NS50.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Members of the public, retailers, employers, Government agencies, the arts community and more, poured forward to contribute to the NS50 commemorations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I recently took over the chairmanship of ACCORD from Dr Mohamad Maliki and was so inspired by the enthusiasm and passion of its members.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is one of those Government committees where members, after serving many years, still say, "Can I please continue serving?", and they do not want to step down!

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Switzer Alliance is one of the participating merchants of this initiative.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The owners felt that they had greatly benefited from their NS experience and wanted to pay it forward – by offering special discounts to NSmen on SAF Day and organising free seminars on topics of interest to NSmen.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin and Assoc Prof Randolph Tan asked about preparing our NSFs for life after NS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Earlier, I talked about improving individuals’ performance in terms of fitness and operational skills.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These are already very basic, useful life skills.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But further, in the process of developing these skills, our NSFs also learn valuable competencies, such as leadership, discipline, resilience and teamwork.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And these are useful qualities that will help our NSFs perform well in their careers after full-time NS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, I always advise male students, of all the leadership programmes that are out there in the market, the best one is the one SAF conducts and that you acquire during NS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: ACCORD will continue to drive this, will continue to work with the industry partners to expand accreditation of NS skills and help employers recognise the value of NS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But having said that, we should be mindful not to lose sight of the fact that, ultimately, NS is about ensuring the operational effectiveness of SAF, it is a service to the nation, and it cannot become transactional.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, in conclusion, we must cherish our current level of support for NS and do whatever we can to maintain or raise it even further.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is psychological defence at its finest, where the entire population lines up behind a national cause.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When our enemies see our resolve and unity, they will think twice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Mr Chairman, as Minister Ng Eng Hen has explained, Singapore is faced with changing geopolitical and threat environments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: With it, the role of SAF is also expanding to respond to these threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: But what do these developments mean for the average Singaporean, for them to appreciate their role in Singapore’s defence?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In today’s open world of porous boundaries and the Internet of Things, aggressors can put pressure on a target nation in many ways, and they have increasingly sought to direct this pressure at ordinary citizens, misleading them into resenting their fellow citizens of a different background, or unsettling their confidence in the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Essentially, a crisis of trust ensues and a society works towards its own unravelling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As such tactics become more commonplace, our people must be willing and ready to resist and respond and build up personal and social resilience to overcome these threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Beyond Military Defence, our leaders recognised that our ability to face and overcome any eventual conflict also depends on our people and their resolve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Indeed, with emerging concerns that target our people’s hearts and minds, individuals play an increasingly critical role as our first defenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Recognising this, MINDEF has both expanded and enriched our outreach over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In the past, our efforts were centred on the annual commemoration of Total Defence Day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Today, we have, in addition to that, a wide array of activities year-round, aimed at helping Singaporeans appreciate our threats and challenges and what they can do in response.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This would not have been possible without our growing pool of partners from the public, private and people sectors that have come on board to work with us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: One of the viewers, 58-year-old housewife Mrs Vemala Gurunathan was struck by the episode on cyberattacks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: She shared, and I quote, "I was quite surprised that attacks on cyberspace can actually cause chaos in our society and everyday life… I like how the programme even showed us how we can overcome this by being more careful online and not blindly believing everything we read".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: I am heartened that, today, Total Defence resonates with Singaporeans, and many are stepping up to contribute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We have also seen how some participants of MINDEF's various engagement programmes have gone on to encourage others to play their part in Total Defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: One of them is 26-year-old Chong Yu Lun.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Yu Lun has participated in every run of MINDEF’s short film competition "ciNE65", creating multiple winning, but more importantly, inspiring entries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: These range from those that encourage NSmen to defend our home, to those that portray the resilience of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: When asked recently about what drives him to make these videos, he said, "I'm very motivated to create films that hopefully Singaporeans would be proud to call their own...we challenge ourselves to create inspiring stories that blend in a subtle element of that little patriotism in us".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Ms Low Yen Ling asked for an update on the 2018 Total Defence Campaign and how it will address new threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon highlighted the need to do so in the face of terrorism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Other threats like fake news and cyberattacks compound this need.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: While the military and civil domains are most intuitively associated with defence, it is increasingly important today that we broaden our definition of what it means to safeguard Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For one, our social cohesion could be compromised if Singaporeans allow themselves to be swayed by divisive falsehoods or stigmatise particular social groups in the wake of a violent attack.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Religion today has been misused by terror groups like ISIS and misrepresented by preachers who espouse extreme views.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Religion has also begun to enter the realm of politics as seen in the region, resulting in built up tensions in community relations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As a society, we can and will continue to be tested.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Upon hearing the news and watching such clips, how would or should Singaporeans react?

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: The immediate reaction could include worry, disbelief, fear, anger and possibly distrust.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: However, these reactions could be mitigated, depending on how strong we are psychologically as individuals, and socially as a community.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: With strong social cohesion and psychological resilience, the Muslims amongst us would reject attempts to sway them to adopt extremist ideas, denouncing those images and assuring their non-Muslim friends and neighbours that the images they saw neither reflect Islam nor Muslims in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Again, with strong social cohesion and psychological resilience, we would also see our non-Muslims who have confidence in their Muslim friends expressing support and giving assurances that what they saw neither represent Islam nor Muslims in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: At the same time, those who might be affected by the images would feel comfortable enough to clarify their doubts and reservations with their Muslim friends.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: With deepened trust, all Singaporeans would stand united to safeguard the harmony we hold dear.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: This is the essence of our Social and Psychological Defence.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Mr Chairman, may I say a few words in Malay, please.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: (In Malay):   Just as we move forward to build up the Next-Gen SAF, we will gear Total Defence towards the new security environment, according greater attention to Social and Psychological Defence.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: While the military and civil domains are most intuitively associated with defence, it is increasingly important today that we broaden our definition of what it means to safeguard Singapore.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Religion has also begun to enter the realm of politics, as seen in the region, resulting in built-up tensions in community relations.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We need only turn to our own history to remind ourselves that trust and goodwill among communities are not a given and must be worked at unceasingly to sustain.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: As a society, we can and will continue to be tested.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Just last year, two propaganda videos featuring an ISIS fighter from Singapore in Syria surfaced – the first was of him rallying others to join him, while the other was more graphic ‒ showing him shooting three men at close range.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Upon hearing such news and watching such clips, how would or should Singaporeans react?

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: The immediate reaction could include worry, disbelief, fear, anger and, possibly, suspicion and distrust.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: However, these reactions could be mitigated, depending on how strong we are psychologically as individuals and socially as a community.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: With strong social cohesion and psychological resilience, the Muslims amongst us would reject attempts to sway them to adopt extremist ideas, denouncing those images and assuring their non-Muslim friends and neighbours that the images they saw neither reflect Islam nor Muslims in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: If we possess strong social cohesion and psychological resilience, we would also see our non-Muslims, who have a lot of confidence in their Muslim friends, expressing support and giving assurances that what they saw neither represent Islam nor Muslims in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: At the same time, those who might be affected by the images would feel comfortable enough to clarify their doubts and reservations with their Muslim friends.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: With deepened trust, all Singaporeans would stand united to safeguard the harmony we hold dear.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: As the Malay saying goes – "United we stand, divided we fall".

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: This is the essence of our Social and Psychological Defence.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: (In English): As Mr Amrin Amin noted, there are also new potential fault lines in our social fabric beyond race and religion which could be used against us if we are not careful.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: With globalisation and significant mobility amongst Singaporeans, we cannot assume that all Singaporean children will continue to experience the culture of our local schools and neighbourhoods as they grow up.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: There are also others who come from transnational families.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: These are not concerns in and of themselves, but they do signal that the experiences and perspectives of our people are more varied than before.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: If we do not continue to forge common understanding, our differences could be played up to divide us, making it difficult for us to band together in a crisis.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: This means growing our common space by interacting with people of different backgrounds, speaking up against attempts to sow discord and helping those in need.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: One important element of this is to fortify trust and understanding among people of different religious backgrounds to guard against radical ideas that may divide us.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: It is also heartening to see that our youths understand the importance of Social Defence, and are initiating ground-up projects to expand our common space, too.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: The Interfaith Youth Circle, for example, was started by a group of youths who wanted to bridge gaps in understanding about the different religions in Singapore, especially given the negative sentiment and online chatter following terror attacks around the world.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: They organise activities, such as scriptural reasoning sessions, where people come together to read and reflect on scriptures from different faiths.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Such efforts foster deeper trust and a stronger will to stand firm against attempts to turn us against one another.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked about the impact of fake news on security, and how MINDEF is combating this threat.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: In an interconnected world, Singaporeans are more easily exposed to pressures that could unsettle their willingness to uphold our national interests, including racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: These influences could come in the form of falsehoods deliberately spread online.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: In 2007, for example, an insensitive prank photo of pork sold at National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) Fairprice with a halal sticker on the packaging was circulated via e-mail.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: NTUC Fairprice had called it out as false back then.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Social media had become a lot more prevalent in the span of just seven years, and the photo made its rounds on Facebook, where posts are easily shared with a wider audience.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: While the incident was resolved, similar cases could tear at our interfaith unity.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Likewise, falsehoods could be spread to weaken our trust in public institutions and confidence in a shared future or incite fear.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Some Members may recall a video that was shared on social media early last year, purportedly showing an explosion in Tuas.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: While a fire did break out, this said footage of the incident was fake.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: The video had, in fact, been uploaded on YouTube multiple times from 2015 onwards and have on separate occasions been labelled as blasts in China, India and France – that same footage.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: If it had not been debunked, the video could have sparked panic and anxiety amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Moreover, the growing number of Singaporeans who pursue work and educational opportunities abroad may have to wrestle with dissenting views more squarely.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Foreign business partners, schoolmates or friends may at times express fundamental disagreements with Singapore's decisions, policies or actions.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: They could even persuade you to adopt their viewpoint at the expense of supporting our national interests.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Psychological resilience on the part of each individual is being decisive in withstanding such pressures.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I read an opinion piece on Total Defence earlier this year, where Channel NewsAsia editor Jaime Ho rightly pointed out how defence today entails Singaporeans "thinking for ourselves" and "standing up for ourselves".

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: This is Psychological Defence – appreciating our vulnerabilities and challenges, advancing our values and interests; being able to spot mistruths; and standing up for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Just as our threats extend beyond the military realm, so must our deterrence.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: In addition to a credible military force, we need a psychologically resilient people, able to withstand crises or viral attacks, and not be rattled.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: If someone comments negatively about Singapore and our immediate response is not to verify the facts but to instead condemn Singapore and, worse, spread the untruths, we are creating for ourselves a hole in our defence that our adversaries would not hesitate to jump at and widen the divide.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I am glad to see that Singaporeans, such as those behind the online site "Confirm?" which runs quizzes on issues relating to Singapore, have taken the initiative to try and help those around them understand our principles, positions and policies better, preventing them from falling prey to fake news and untruths.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I have elaborated on Social and Psychological Defence because threats in these domains are very real, but often unapparent.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: They have a creeping yet significant impact on our ability to defend Singapore.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: In the other pillars of our Total Defence, Singaporeans are our first defenders, too.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Enlisting in SAFVC is one way many women, new citizens and first-generation Permanent Residents have stepped up to serve.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: To prevent a terror attack, for example, Mr Charnjit Singh, Chairman of the Community Emergency and Engagement Committee (C2E) in Telok Blangah, worked with other volunteers to conduct regular patrols on our trains.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: In MINDEF and SAF, we are equipping our personnel to respond to crises in their personal capacity, too.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Most of our servicemen who undergo BMT learn some first aid and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)-automated external defibrillator (AED) skills, as do our SAFVC.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Mr Rajendran Mathan Prasath is a commendable example of someone who has not only stepped up to do more for Military Defence by joining SAFVC, but used the skills acquired during his training to contribute to Civil Defence while off duty.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: In April last year, he performed CPR on an elderly lady suffering a cardiac arrest.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: It complements the SG Secure effort and better prepares our servicemen to be active community responders.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: MINDEF, alongside our partners, will continue to encourage different groups of Singaporeans to contribute in concrete ways to Total Defence.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We are constantly exploring innovative ways to engage our youths.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng asked how we are doing so.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Mr Mohamed Shahmir Anwar, a secondary school teacher who facilitated the game and conducted reflection sessions for his students, shared that the students both enjoyed it and learnt valuable lessons on Total Defence.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: To quote him, "This game is something different, something exciting...the students want to try it because it is interactive…Because the games are so relatable to them, it is a good platform to teach them about Total Defence".

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Other interactive tools to bring Total Defence to life for our youths include a Total Defence puzzle that was developed in collaboration with agencies across the Government and creatives at Singapore Press Holdings (SPH) THINK.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: It has been distributed to schools, SAF camps and community centres (CCs).

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Various organisations, especially schools, have found the puzzle to be a useful learning resource.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: MINDEF also has more specific programmes for our young recruits.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I fully agree with Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef that besides physical training, it is important to prepare our recruits psychologically in a changing security environment.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Beyond engaging future recruits as part of our outreach to students, there is a comprehensive plan to strengthen their physical and psychological resilience when they enlist.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: This is infused in various aspects of the full-time NS experience.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: As they march past iconic landmarks in Singapore, they are reminded of what they are training to protect.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: The soldiers march to their graduation parade at Marina Bay today.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: It represents their resolve to never again let Singapore fall.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Besides these events and activities, it is the overall full-time NS experience – building strong bonds with their mates and commanders and experiencing values in action demonstrated by their commanders – that strengthens our recruits psychologically.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: With understanding and conviction come the resilience to protect our home even in the face of new threats and challenges.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Families are key pillars of support for our NSmen.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Ms Joan Pereira had asked what MINDEF is doing to engage families.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Through ACCORD, we also partner organisations, such as Families for Life and the Centre for Fathering, to engage families on NS and Total Defence.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Mr Chairman, may I have your indulgence to continue a little bit longer?

speaker: The Chairman
text: As we do still have some time before the guillotine time for MINDEF, please wrap up in the next few minutes.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Activities we have had include the "Celebrating NS50" picnic and Dads for Life Camp last year.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: ACCORD has also conducted focus group discussions with women to gather feedback on how we can better support our servicemen and their families.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: In this way, families can not only support NSmen in their NS journey but appreciate the role they themselves play in Total Defence, too.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Besides the individuals that I have highlighted today, there are many others who are putting Total Defence into action in their everyday lives, by giving their best during NS training, securing their personal devices, learning first aid, donating blood, and taking up new skills.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: MINDEF will continually work towards strengthening this whole-of-society effort.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: With a strong Total Defence, we have every reason to be hopeful and confident in Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can the Minister share more details on the size and nature of our deployment to Iraq, what tasks our troops would undertake, and what and whose resources they can call upon to assure their security there?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Chairman, those were good questions and very relevant ones.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: What is our threat assessment when we send SAF troops to missions?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, whether we send them to Afghanistan, whether we send them to Iraq, whether we send them to the Gulf of Aden, even when we send them to Timor-Leste − peacekeeping operations − we have casualties in peacekeeping operations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We do this because, at the core, you are protecting Singapore's interests.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Whether it is imagery analysts, or weapons locating radar, we made a contribution.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We identified even hotspots for the coalition and the terrorist threat disappeared for now.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I say "for now" because we are keeping a watch on Al Qaeda cells and there is every possibility that there can be a resurgence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think just two or even three years ago, if you just look at the geographical map, the areas in which ISIS strongholds controlled, were a majority of Iraq and Syria.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, there are a few last strongholds, if any.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: How do we prepare servicemen for these threats?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Then, not only the elements that are required to fulfil the operations – we will talk about that because the Member asked about it – but the protection is necessary.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You can minimise it but you will never completely eliminate it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Against ISIS, it has been relatively shorter, I think since 2014.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But for us to not continue to contribute when the more significant gains have been actually taking back Iraq, I think it is not within our character and not within our mission imperative.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The central mission is so that ground zero for the export of terrorists must be eliminated as we did in Afghanistan.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Just imagine if we said, "Well, the rest of the world can go about it but we don't worry about Afghanistan." If the problems there gain momentum, we will suffer.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For Iraq, for ISIS, we have a much more vested interest because there were foreign fighters from Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore who were there.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The first phase was actually the most difficult − to recover territory, to rid ISIS of their resources, of their ability to increase their resources to export terrorism.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: While our chaps were there, we were very useful.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are now deployed with other troops, the Australians and some other troops, for which there is joint protection and we can call on them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I visited our troops last year and was satisfied that, to the extent possible, there is perimeter protection.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the event of an incident, there will be measures to respond to that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, when I was there, it just so happened that they were responding in a simulated scenario to an attack.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Americans were there, the Australians were there, our chaps were there, and they mobilised the hospitals and then, for how to guard the vicinity.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think that is about as much as I can say for all the questions but let me just summarise.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We dealt with the threat after 9-11, Bali bomb blast and joined other forces in Afghanistan.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Somebody said "Communism without divine intervention, without God, took 50 years."

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: This is more about Singaporeans who form part of international humanitarian teams or respond to international humanitarian activities around the world, whether it is war-related or natural disaster-related.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: These are people who are disaster, medically and also tactically trained; they can actually value add to the response of a crisis that we have.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It came about because we recognised that after Cyclone Nargis, after Nepal, the first two to three days after an incident occurs are where you have the least coordinated response, even if all the resources are there.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, for instance, if you remember the typhoon in the Philippines, we sent a C-130.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The reason they were under-utilised was that there were no air command and control facilities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Only the Americans could because I think they had their aircraft carrier and they were able to control the airspace.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have linked up with other humanitarian organisations and I think we had one or two equivalents of table-top exercises to, say, if something happens, whom do I contact?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We offered for these civil groups, these volunteer groups, to be physically based in Changi, if they can spare.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We just have to keep increasing our contacts, increasing our efficiency and when the next crisis strikes, I think Singapore can play a more definitive role and contribute more.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This clarification is in relation to the unconventional threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I think Senior Minister of State Mohamad Maliki painted quite a graphic picture of the threats these provide.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: My concern was whether we should be doing more.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: First of all, in relation to the video on terrorism, for 99% of people, they will be disgusted by that video.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: But there might be a very tiny percentage, 0.001%, and perhaps a lone wolf who would be inspired by it to commit acts of violence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Notwithstanding how strong our psychological defence is, all it takes is one person to get influenced by it to carry out the terror attack.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The countervailing risk, of course, is that other people may generalise and say, "This is what Muslims do" which, I think in Singapore, that is not a big issue.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Obviously, it is divisive because it suggests NTUC trying to sell pork to Muslims.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: But then it surfaced again six or seven years later.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: But this shows the power of fake news.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Fake news is sensational, therefore, it gets circulated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: So, the truth is almost always triumphed by fake news.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Could we take further steps to identify the creators of these fake news and take other actions against them?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: But if we can eliminate the virus, that is even better.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We totally agree with what we need to do to ensure that there is a comprehensive response to all these unconventional threats, whether it is images or otherwise.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Just one image may create reactions in different groups of people and it is important for us to be aware of the reaction that different groups of Singaporeans may have and, therefore, what we need to do to strengthen our resolve first.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, the different groups of people and different players of stakeholders that are relevant in this context: one, at an individual level, we need to be consistent, we need to be aware of our own reactions and how much do we take forward steps to learn more about such issues as well as build trust and relationship with all the other communities so that if something like that happens, we are not easily rattled.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We ask questions, we ask and look for the facts rather than react negatively.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: If you see various legislation, various discussions in this House, you can see many things are happening.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: The development of the cyber defence agencies is one effort that looks at some of the areas that we need to do in the cyber domain.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We also need to start looking at how Singaporeans respond to such fake news on social media.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: And this is one of the biggest challenges − the skillsets required by individuals to respond to such social media platforms.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Once you see something on your Facebook feed or once you get something from your WhatsApp group, what do you do?

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: That is where we need to help Singaporeans to understand the different ecosystems that exist, the environment that exists.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: It is an environment that is evolving, as we speak.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, today, it is critical for us to educate Singaporeans in every age group, not just adults, but young children.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
